cells.note: Systematic-review synthesis of studies conducted in varied surgical educational and performance settings; the study text does not specify participant ages or a common duration.

cells.quote: Previous studies suggest that adopting a student-focused approach to teaching correlates positively with HE teachers’ self-efficacy beliefs [9,10] and positive emotions [11], indicating its potential relevance for their well-being as well.
cells.note: Background association attributed to prior studies; this protocol reports no new data or printed effect size for the association.

cells.quote: This review includes studies of a wide range of procedure skill training studies and shows that 15/17 studies have the similar conclusion, that training with an HF simulator does not have outcomes superior to training with an LF simulator.
cells.note: The review reports similar or non-superior outcomes, but does not report an equivalence test or adequate power; therefore direction is coded ns rather than 0.

cells.quote: Review of laparoscopic surgery skill training studies showed that 8/8 concluded that training with an HF simulator did not have outcomes superior to training with LF simulators.
cells.note: This is a subgroup synthesis of eight laparoscopic studies; no equivalence test or adequate power is reported.

cells.quote: These five studies found similar outcomes with LF and HF simulators and that either LF or HF had better outcomes than a control group with no intervention or a group that received didactic training only.
cells.note: The comparison pooled low- and high-fidelity simulation against no intervention or didactic-only control.

O.outcome_detail: skill transfer for junior and senior residents

cells.quote: The authors found that both junior and senior residents had better skill transfer from the bench model to the live animal model after practicing on HF simulators compared to LF simulators.
cells.note: This finding came from one of the 17 reviewed studies and was reported separately by training level.

cells.quote: With regard to “breathing control” (p = 0.012), “continuous chest compression while charging the defibrillator” (p = 0.017), “electrocardiogram analysis” (p = 0.021) and “time interval between electric shocks” (p = 0.016), students in the LF group performed significantly better.

cells.note: The study reports no significant between-group difference but does not report an equivalence test or adequate-power basis for coding equivalence.

O.outcome_detail: performance in simulated ventricular-fibrillation ALS scenario

cells.quote: Performance, as assessed by video analysis, was comparable between groups, but, unexpectedly, the low-fidelity group had significantly better results in several sub-items.
cells.note: The low-fidelity group was significantly better on breathing control, continuous chest compression while charging the defibrillator, electrocardiogram analysis, and time interval between electric shocks; most other criteria were comparable.

O.outcome_detail: self-rated confidence and perceived performance relative to actual performance

cells.quote: In this study, participants using HF simulator-training were prone to overrate their abilities and performance, despite showing similar outcomes in theoretical testing and similar, or even inferior, performance of practical skills.
cells.note: The high-fidelity group showed overconfidence: confidence increased without an equivalent increase in knowledge or skill.

O.outcome_detail: belief in learning advantage and fear of being disadvantaged

cells.quote: Before the course (69%) the majority of students in the HF group assumed that they had a significant advantage with regards to their individual learning success, compared to students in the LF group. Participation in the course had no effect on this assumption: 53% of students in the HF group were still convinced of their individual benefit. The difference between pre- and post-course was not statistically significant (p = 0.052). In contrast, we found a significant reduction concerning their fear of being disadvantaged between pre-course (37%) and post-course (13%) (p = 0.003) in the LF group.
cells.note: The reported pre/post findings differ by group: the HF group's perceived advantage did not significantly change, whereas the LF group's fear of disadvantage decreased significantly.
